cues.text: Chapter four: file organisation.
Let us begin with what a database file physically is.
Physical files consist of pages, which are also called blocks, and these pages hold records.
Now, records come in two broad kinds.
Fixed-length records have predictable offsets.
Because every record is the same size, the system can calculate exactly where the third record, or the three-hundredth, begins within a page.
Variable-length records are different, since their sizes vary, and so they may use slot directories.
A slot directory is a small table that keeps track of where each record sits inside the page, so the system can still find records even though their lengths differ.
Next, the buffer manager.
Buffer managers cache pages in memory.
Instead of going to storage every time a page is needed, the database keeps recently used pages in memory.
And this brings us to the central idea of the chapter: file organisation determines how records are placed and located.
In other words, it is the strategy that decides where a record goes when you store it, and how the system finds it again later.
The source now compares five organisations in a table.
The columns are the organisation, its mechanism, its benefit, and its limitation.
I will take the rows in order.
First, the heap.
Its mechanism is unordered pages.
Its benefit is fast inserts, because a new record can simply go wherever there is room.
Its limitation is that a search may scan all pages, since nothing tells you where a record is.
Second, sequential, or sorted, organisation.
Its mechanism is that records are ordered by key.
The benefit is efficient ordered and range access, meaning it is good when you want records in key order, or all records within a range of key values.
The limitation is that inserts may require movement, because a new record has to go in its proper place in the order.
Third, hash organisation.
The mechanism is that a hash key maps to buckets.
The benefit is efficient equality lookup, which means finding a record whose key equals a given value.
The limitations are collisions, where different keys land in the same bucket, and poor range access, because hashing does not keep keys in any useful order.
Fourth, indexed sequential.
The mechanism is an ordered file plus an index.
The benefit is that you get both sequential and indexed access.
The limitation is maintenance overhead, since both the file and its index must be kept up to date.
Fifth, clustered organisation.
The mechanism is that related records are stored near one another.
The benefit is locality for range and join workloads, because records likely to be needed together are physically close.
The limitations are reorganisation, and limited clustering choices.
A given set of records can only be physically arranged in so many ways, so you cannot cluster for every purpose at once.
Now the final block, which covers sorting, input and output costs, and maintenance.
External sorting divides data into memory-sized sorted runs, then merges those runs.
So when data is too large to sort in memory at once, the system sorts it in memory-sized pieces, each called a sorted run, and then merges the runs together into one sorted result.
On cost, the source says random I/O usually costs more than sequential I/O, and that SSD characteristics differ from spinning disks.
So the usual rule, that sequential access beats random access, is worth keeping in mind, but the source notes that solid state drives behave differently from spinning disks.
The source also warns that fragmentation, page splits and dead versions may increase maintenance work.
Fragmentation is when storage becomes scattered or inefficiently used.
Page splits happen when a page becomes full and must be divided.
Dead versions are old record versions that are no longer needed but still occupy space.
Each of these may add to the maintenance the system has to do.
Finally, a point that is easy to forget: physical row order is not guaranteed in SQL without ORDER BY.
Even if rows happen to be stored in a certain order, you must not rely on that.
If you need results in a particular order, you must ask for it explicitly with an ORDER BY clause.
